message.content:
Lions (Panthera leo) and zebras (Equus quagga) belong to two very different mammalian orders—Carnivora for the lion and Perissodactyla for the zebra. Their lineages split deep in the evolutionary tree, so the most recent common ancestor (MRCA) of the two species is not a familiar animal but an early, small, probably insectivorous mammal that lived in the Paleocene (roughly 60–70 million years ago).

That ancestor would have been a member of the clade **Laurasiatheria**, the group that gave rise to many modern mammalian orders including Carnivora, Perissodactyla, Cetartiodactyla, Chiroptera, and others. In other words, the MRCA of lions and zebras was a primitive, early Laurasiatherian mammal that existed before the diversification of the major mammalian clades that eventually led to cats and horses.

They diverged earlier. The common ancestor would be a mammal from the clade Laurasiatheria, maybe the last common ancestor of the clades that gave rise to Carnivora and Perissodactyla. That would be a mammal from the order of early ungulate-like mammals, maybe the last common ancestor of the clade that includes both. That ancestor would be a small, probably insectivorous mammal from the Paleocene. But we can say: The last common ancestor of lions and zebras lived around 60-70 million years ago, likely a small, omnivorous mammal that gave rise to the Laurasiatherian mammals.
